facts.text: I asked what an article says about AI regulation.
The article discusses the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).
The GDPR is an EU regulation on data protection and privacy in the EU and the European Economic Area (EEA).
The GDPR was made by the European Parliament and Council of the European Union.
The GDPR has journal reference L119, 4 May 2016, p. 1–88.
The GDPR was dated as made on 14 April 2016.
The GDPR implementation date is 25 May 2018.
The GDPR became enforceable beginning 25 May 2018.
The GDPR is directly binding and applicable because it is a regulation, not a directive.
The GDPR addresses transfer of personal data outside the EU and EEA areas.
The GDPR primary aim is to enhance individuals' control and rights over their personal data and simplify the regulatory environment for international business.
The GDPR applies to enterprises processing personal information of individuals located in the EEA.
The article states that as of 6 October 2022 the United Kingdom retains the law in identical form despite no longer being an EU member state.
The article states that the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) was adopted on 28 June 2018.
The article says the GDPR contains provisions and requirements related to processing personal data of individuals called data subjects located in the EEA.
The article says the GDPR has eleven chapters.
The article says the GDPR applies if the data controller, processor, or data subject is based in the EU.
The article says the GDPR can apply to organizations based outside the EU if they collect or process personal data of individuals located inside the EU under certain circumstances.
The article says the GDPR does not apply to processing of data by a person for a purely personal or household activity with no connection to a professional or commercial activity.
The article states that personal data is information that relates to an identified or identifiable individual.
The article states that the GDPR includes Article 4 definitions for personal data, processing, data subject, controller, and processor.
The article mentions Article 48 regarding judgments and decisions of third countries requiring transfer or disclosure of personal data.
The article says the GDPR includes a risk-based approach as an enforcement method.
The article says the risk-based approach shifts the duty to controllers for ensuring compliance.
The article says data controllers must evaluate risks at each stage of the data life cycle.

The article says data controllers implement the risk-based approach through data protection impact assessments (Article 35) and notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority (Article 33).
The article lists lawful bases in Article 6(a)-(f) including consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, and legitimate interests.
The article says consent must be explicit for data collected and each purpose data is used for when consent is the lawful basis.
The article says consent must be specific, freely-given, plainly-worded, and unambiguous.
The article says an online form with consent options structured as an opt-out selected by default is a violation of the GDPR.
The article says multiple types of processing may not be bundled into a single affirmation prompt.
The article says data subjects must be allowed to withdraw consent at any time and the process must not be harder than opting in.
The article says a data controller may not refuse service to users who decline consent to processing that is not strictly necessary to use the service.
The article says consent for children is required and defines children as less than 16 years old, with an option for member states to set it as low as 13.
The article says Article 12 requires controllers to provide information in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form using clear and plain language, especially for children.
The article says Article 15 gives a right of access to personal data and information about how it is processed.
The article says Article 20 provides a right to data portability.
The article says Article 17 provides a right to erasure and mentions a 30-day timeframe.
The article says Article 21 allows individuals to object to processing personal information for marketing or non-service related purposes.
The article says data controllers must inform individuals of their right to object from the first communication.
The article says data controllers must allow objections to be considered individually when requests are manifestly unfounded or excessive.
The article says data protection officers (DPOs) are required in certain cases including public authorities (with exceptions) and regular and systematic monitoring on a large scale.
The article says DPOs must have expert knowledge of data protection law and practices.
The article says DPO contact details must be published and registered with the supervisory authority.
The article says businesses must report data breaches to national supervisory authorities within 72 hours if they have an adverse effect on user privacy.
The article says violators may be fined up to €20 million or up to 4% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is greater.
The article says Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default.
The article says pseudonymisation is a required process for stored data under the GDPR definition described.
The article says pseudonymisation transforms personal data so it cannot be attributed to a specific data subject without additional information.
The article says encryption is an example of pseudonymisation that cannot be reversed without the correct decryption key.
The article says tokenisation replaces sensitive data with non-sensitive substitutes called tokens.
The article says records of processing activities must be maintained under Article 30 when employing more than 250 people or when processing is likely to result in risk, among other criteria.
The article says records shall be in electronic form and made available to the supervisory authority on request.
The article says Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and sets a maximum of 72 hours after becoming aware of a data breach.
The article says individuals have to be notified if a high risk of adverse impact is determined under Article 34.

The article says notice to data subjects is not required if the controller has implemented appropriate technical and organisational protection measures such as encryption that render personal data unintelligible to unauthorized persons.
The article says non-EU establishments subject to GDPR must appoint an EU Representative under Article 27.
The article says the EU Representative serves as a point of contact for GDPR obligations.
The article says the non-EU establishment must issue a duly signed document designating the EU Representative.

The article says failure to designate an EU Representative is considered ignorance of the regulation and is a violation subject to fines up to €10 million or up to 2% of annual worldwide turnover, whichever is greater.

The article says the GDPR forbids transfer of personal data of EU data subjects to countries outside the EEA unless appropriate safeguards are imposed or the third country's data protection regulations are considered adequate by the European Commission (Article 45).

The article says the GDPR applies extraterritorially to non-EU controllers and processors when offering goods or services to data subjects in the EEA or monitoring their behaviour in the EEA (Article 3(2)).
The article says the UK granted royal assent to the Data Protection Act 2018 on 23 May 2018.
The article says the UK formally withdrew from the European Union on 31 January 2020.
The article says the UK remained subject to EU law including GDPR until the end of the transition period on 31 December 2020.
The article says in April 2019 the UK Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) issued a proposed code of practice for social networking services when used by minors.
The article says in March 2021 Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Oliver Dowden stated the UK was exploring divergence from the EU GDPR.
The article mentions a Deloitte 2018 study stating 92% of companies believe they are able to comply with GDPR in the long run.
The article says a typical disclaimer is not sufficient to gain assumed consent to record calls under GDPR consent rules.
The article says over 80 percent of surveyed IT professionals expected GDPR-related spending to be at least US$100,000.

The article says a report commissioned by Baker & McKenzie found around 70 percent of respondents believe organizations need to invest additional budget/effort to comply with consent, data mapping, and cross-border data transfer requirements.
The article estimates total cost for EU companies at around €200 billion and for US companies at $41.7 billion.
The article says the GDPR has been criticized for potential administrative burden and unclear compliance requirements.
The article says there is concern about GDPR implementation in blockchain systems because blockchain transactions are transparent and fixed.
The article mentions a 'right to explanation' of algorithmic decisions and says legal scholars argued its existence is unclear and limited.
The article says Mark Zuckerberg called GDPR a 'very positive for the Internet' and called for GDPR-style laws to be adopted in the US.
The article says the regulation was adopted on 14 April 2016 and entered into force on 24 May 2016.
The article says the GDPR entered into force 20 days after its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union on 24 May 2016.
The article says the GDPR became valid in EEA countries Iceland, Liechtenstein, and Norway on 20 July 2018.
The article says the GDPR provisions became directly applicable in all member states on 25 May 2018.
The article says the proposal for the GDPR was released on 25 January 2012.
The article says the European Parliament Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs (LIBE) had its orientation vote on 21 October 2013.
The article says negotiations between the European Parliament, Council and Commission resulted in a joint proposal on 15 December 2015.
The article says the European Parliament's LIBE Committee voted for negotiations on 17 December 2015.
The article says adoption by the Council of the European Union occurred on 8 April 2016.
The article says the only member state voting against the Council adoption was Austria.
The article says the European Parliament adopted the GDPR on 14 April 2016.
The article says the GDPR became enforceable beginning 25 May 2018.

The article says Facebook and subsidiaries WhatsApp and Instagram, and Google LLC targeting Android, were sued by Max Schrems's non-profit NOYB just hours after midnight on 25 May 2018 for forced consent.
The article says on 21 January 2019 Google was fined €50 million by the French DPA for showing insufficient control, consent, and transparency for behavioural advertising.

The article says in July 2019 the British Information Commissioner's Office issued an intention to fine British Airways a record £183 million for poor security arrangements enabling a 2018 web skimming attack affecting around 380,000 transactions.
The article says British Airways was ultimately fined a reduced amount of £20 million.
The article says in December 2019 Politico reported Ireland and Luxembourg faced significant backlogs in investigations of major foreign companies under GDPR.
The article says in March 2021 EU member states led by France were reported to be attempting to modify the impact of the privacy regulation by exempting national security agencies.
The article says after around 160 million Euros in GDPR fines were imposed in 2020, the figure was already over one billion Euros in 2021.
The article says the California Consumer Privacy Act took effect on 1 January 2020.
The article says Virginia passed the Consumer Data Protection Act on 2 March 2021.
The article says Colorado enacted the Colorado Privacy Act on 8 July 2021.
The article says the Republic of Turkey adopted the Law on The Protection of Personal Data on 24 March 2016.
The article says China's Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) came into force in 2021.

The article mentions that in 2020 the European Commission assessed that 69% of the population above age 16 in the EU had heard about the GDPR and 71% had heard about their national data protection authority.
The article says the GDPR and the NIS Directive all apply from 25 May 2018 as part of the EU Digital Single Market strategy.

British Airways £183 million intention to fine July 2019
data protection by design and by default Article 25
